title: AI & the Future of Workplace Learning: Rethinking Why & How We Develop Talent
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Melissa Muth Martinez argues that when AI makes information instantly available, workplace learning built on knowledge transfer and recall is no longer the right target; the scarce thing is judgment, the ability to decide, curate and implement. She notes that such skills grow through practice, feedback, ambiguous situations and debriefing, not courses, and warns that offloading cognitive work to AI may erode the very abilities now prized. She calls for changes in how learning is designed, how managers develop people and how individuals think about growth. The post ends by recasting talent development professionals through seven roles, from strategist to culture carrier, and urges them to rethink their role rather than bolt AI onto the old model.
points: If AI can retrieve and synthesize information in seconds, the training model of information in and retention out loses its rationale and the bar shifts to judgment.
Judgment and critical thinking develop through practice, feedback and debriefing in situations without obvious answers, which is a coaching culture rather than a calendar of events.
Developing judgment requires managers to give real-stakes problems and psychological safety, which is an organizational design problem.
There is a risk that outsourcing thinking to AI atrophies judgment, leaving people better at prompting but not at deciding.
The author recasts talent development as a seven-role function, including strategist, curator, connector and experimentalist, rather than a content-production shop.
quotes: If I can ask an AI tool a question and get a synthesized, contextualized, reasonably accurate answer in under ten seconds, then the argument for designing learning primarily around information transfer becomes quite difficult to sustain. The information isn’t scarce anymore. What becomes scarce, and genuinely valuable, is the unique ability to take that knowledge and do something meaningful with it.

Skills like judgment, critical thinking, and the ability to navigate ambiguity don’t develop through information delivery, but through practice, feedback, being put in situations where the answer isn’t obvious and you just have to work through it, and debriefing with someone who can challenge your thinking. Call it what you want—a coaching model maybe?

Developing someone’s judgment means giving them hard problems with real stakes, staying close enough to debrief what happened, and creating the psychological safety for them to make calls that don’t always land perfectly. This is an entirely different job than managing performance or delegating tasks, and most people managers weren’t hired or developed for it. This right here is fundamentally an organizational design problem.

In a world where information is everywhere and infinitely accessible, the design question shifts from “what content do we create” to “what conditions do we create.” The job of those developing people increasingly involves shaping the learning environment, which includes curating the experiences, conversations, challenges, and feedback loops that develop judgment in context, rather than delivering information in isolation.

AI cannot replicate the learning that happens when two people are working through a hard problem together, when a peer names something we couldn’t see in ourselves or when a mentor pushes back on a decision you were confident about and you realize you were missing something. The role of facilitating human connection across teams, levels, and functions—creating the conditions for that kind of learning to happen—becomes significantly more valuable as AI assumes more of our individual cognitive work.

This means the job right now is less about building a definitive program that we get locked into for years and more about running fast experiments, paying close attention to what they reveal, and then iterating on what you find.
